The `date` command printed "Sat Oct  3 05:12:18 PM EDT 2026". That is the system's current local time, shown as day of week, month, day, 12-hour time, time zone, and year. The "EDT" shows the machine is set to Eastern Daylight Time, which is four hours behind UTC. The time also matches the timestamp in the environment context, so the clock looks accurate.

Server clocks drift because each one keeps time with a quartz crystal oscillator, and those crystals aren't perfectly precise. Temperature changes, aging hardware, and variation in manufacturing can all make the oscillator run slightly fast or slow. In virtual machines the problem is worse, because the hypervisor may pause or delay a guest's timer interrupts. Left uncorrected, these small errors add up to noticeable differences over hours or days. That is why servers usually run NTP or a similar service to sync regularly against more accurate reference clocks.
